# z3 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/z3/^0.20.2/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#z3)Z3

Z3 is a theorem prover [from Microsoft Research](https://github.com/Z3Prover/z3/).

This library aims to provide an idiomatic Rust wrapper around Z3.

[§](https://docs.rs#basic-usage)Basic Usage

The simplest way to use Z3 is to build a formula (also known as an [ Ast](https://docs.rs/ast/trait.Ast.html))
and use Z3’s

[to find solutions to it.](https://docs.rs/struct.Solver.html)

`Solver`This example walks through the process of expressing a simple math problem in the language of SMT, asserting it into a Solver, and extracting answers from it. Z3 can encode much more varied and complex problems than this example shows (and some of these features are supported by the Rust bindings), but this covers the absolute basics.

Consider the following problem:

Three friends, named Alice, Bob, and Charlie, wish to divide 30 apples amongst themselves, subject to the following constraints:

- Everyone must get at least one apple.
- All apples must be accounted for.
- Alice must receive at least 5 apples.
- Bob must receive an even number of apples.
- Charlie must get at least as many apples as Bob.
- The number of apples Alice receives must be exactly 3 times more than the number Charlie receives.
What are the possible distributions of apples they could make?

To express this in Z3, we define symbolic `Int`[ Ast](https://docs.rs/ast/trait.Ast.html)s representing the number
of apples each friend has, and

[the constraints of the problem into a](https://docs.rs/struct.Solver.html#method.assert)

`assert`[. We can then query the](https://docs.rs/struct.Solver.html)

`Solver`[for a solution:](https://docs.rs/struct.Solver.html)

`Solver````
 // define Int values representing the number of apples each friend has
 let alice = Int::fresh_const("alice");
 let bob = Int::fresh_const("bob");
 let charlie = Int::fresh_const("charlie");
 // instantiate a Solver
 let solver = Solver::new();
 // encode the constraints of the problem as Bool-valued Asts
 // and assert them in the solver
 solver.assert((&alice + &bob + &charlie).eq(30));
 solver.assert(alice.gt(0));
 solver.assert(bob.gt(0));
 solver.assert(charlie.gt(0));
 solver.assert(alice.ge(5));
 solver.assert((&bob % 2).eq(0));
 solver.assert(charlie.ge(&bob));
 solver.assert(alice.eq(&charlie * 3));
 // iterate over the solutions to our variables
 for solution in solver
     .solutions([alice, bob, charlie], false)
     // we use take to ensure that this loop terminates in case there are very many solutions
     .take(100) {
     // extract concrete values for each modeled Int Ast
     let solution: Vec<u64> = solution.iter().map(Int::as_u64).map(Option::unwrap).collect();
     let alice = solution[0];
     let bob = solution[1];
     let charlie = solution[2];
     println!("alice: {alice}, bob: {bob}, charlie: {charlie}");
     // check that the concrete values match the constraints we gave the solver
     assert_eq!(alice + bob + charlie, 30);
     assert!(alice >= 5);
     assert_eq!(bob % 2, 0);
     assert!(charlie >= bob);
     assert_eq!(alice, charlie * 3);
 }
```
In this case, there are 2 solutions, and the above snippet gives the following output:

`alice: 21, bob: 2, charlie: 7`

`alice: 18, bob: 6, charlie: 6`

# ordeal - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/ordeal/0.4.0/target-redirect/ordeal/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#ordeal)Ordeal

`ordeal` (meaning “verdict / judgment”) is a specialized,
**certificate-checked** QF_BV SMT solver for the [PulseEngine](https://github.com/pulseengine) toolchain. It
exists to replace the Z3 static-link build pain that loom (verified WASM
optimizer) and synth (verified WASM→ARM codegen) carry today — grounding:
loom issue #246.

[§](https://docs.rs#design-in-one-paragraph)Design in one paragraph

An **untrusted solver** emits a machine-checkable **LRAT UNSAT
certificate**; a small **formally-verified checker** validates it. Only the
checker is trusted (the CompCert certifying-algorithm pattern; blueprint =
Lean 4 `bv_decide`, OOPSLA 2025). Z3 is demoted to a differential *oracle*
and benchmark *rival*, not the production engine. The pipeline is: term
graph → bit-blast → AIG → CNF (Tseitin) → SAT → LRAT → verified checker.

[§](https://docs.rs#modules)Modules

- `term`
- `lowering`- `bvnot`,- `bvneg`,- `bvrotl`,- `bvurem`,- `bvsdiv`,- `bvsrem`) built over the closed core, for the ops synth-verify emits but the fragment omits (DES-018).
- `solver`- `check-sat`interface and result types.
- `eval`
- `aig`
- `blast`
- `cnf`
- `sat`
- `lrat`- `ordeal-lrat`crate (the sole trusted component) validates it before any- `Unsat`is returned.
- [`oracle`] — the Z3 differential oracle (behind the`oracle`feature).

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use solver::`- [Certificate](https://docs.rs/solver/struct.Certificate.html);
- `pub use solver::`- [CheckResult](https://docs.rs/solver/enum.CheckResult.html);
- `pub use solver::`- [Model](https://docs.rs/solver/struct.Model.html);
- `pub use solver::`- [Solver](https://docs.rs/solver/struct.Solver.html);
- `pub use term::`- [BoolTerm](https://docs.rs/term/enum.BoolTerm.html);
- `pub use term::`- [BvTerm](https://docs.rs/term/enum.BvTerm.html);
- `pub use term::`- [Sort](https://docs.rs/term/struct.Sort.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules-1)

- [aig](https://docs.rs/aig/index.html)
- And-Inverter Graph with structural hashing and constant folding (DES-002).
- [blast](https://docs.rs/blast/index.html)
- Bit-blasting rules: each QF_BV operation lowered to AIG gates (DES-005..DES-009), one module per op family.
- [cnf](https://docs.rs/cnf/index.html)
- CNF representation and the Tseitin encoder (DES-003).
- [eval](https://docs.rs/eval/index.html)
- Concrete evaluator for the closed QF_BV fragment — the executable SMT-LIB semantics (DES-001).
- [lowering](https://docs.rs/lowering/index.html)
- Derived-op lowering helpers (DES-018 / TR-015).
- [lrat](https://docs.rs/lrat/index.html)
- LRAT certificate emission from the CDCL proof trace (DES-013).
- [sat](https://docs.rs/sat/index.html)
- The pure-Rust CDCL SAT core (DES-004) — primary engine on every target.
- [sliver](https://docs.rs/sliver/index.html)
- The loom array/UF sliver (P3) — an extended query layer that is
**preprocessed away**into the closed QF_BV core before bit-blasting.
- [solver](https://docs.rs/solver/index.html)
- The one-shot solver interface and the P1 pipeline dispatcher (DES-012).
- [term](https://docs.rs/term/index.html)
- The `ordeal`term language: the closed QF_BV fragment from loom issue #246.

# lib.rs - source

# ordeal/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)//! # Ordeal
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//!
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//! `ordeal` (meaning "verdict / judgment") is a specialized,
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//! **certificate-checked** QF_BV SMT solver for the [PulseEngine] toolchain. It
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//! exists to replace the Z3 static-link build pain that loom (verified WASM
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//! optimizer) and synth (verified WASM→ARM codegen) carry today — grounding:
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//! loom issue #246.
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//!
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//! ## Design in one paragraph
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//!
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//! An **untrusted solver** emits a machine-checkable **LRAT UNSAT
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//! certificate**; a small **formally-verified checker** validates it. Only the
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//! checker is trusted (the CompCert certifying-algorithm pattern; blueprint =
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//! Lean 4 `bv_decide`, OOPSLA 2025). Z3 is demoted to a differential *oracle*
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//! and benchmark *rival*, not the production engine. The pipeline is: term
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//! graph → bit-blast → AIG → CNF (Tseitin) → SAT → LRAT → verified checker.
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//!
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//! ## Modules
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//!
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//! - [`term`] — the closed QF_BV fragment (the exact loom #246 op set).
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//! - [`lowering`] — blessed derived-op constructors (`bvnot`, `bvneg`,
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//!   `bvrotl`, `bvurem`, `bvsdiv`, `bvsrem`) built over the closed core, for
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//!   the ops synth-verify emits but the fragment omits (DES-018).
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//! - [`solver`] — the one-shot `check-sat` interface and result types.
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//! - [`eval`] — the concrete evaluator (executable SMT-LIB semantics; the
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//!   test oracle for every blasting rule and the SAT-model self-check).
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//! - [`aig`] — the And-Inverter Graph arena (structural hashing, folding).
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//! - [`blast`] — per-op-family bit-blasting rules (term → AIG).
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//! - [`cnf`] — CNF types and the Tseitin encoder (AIG → CNF).
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//! - [`sat`] — the pure-Rust CDCL core (primary engine on every target).
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//! - [`lrat`] — LRAT certificate emission from the CDCL proof trace; the
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//!   `ordeal-lrat` crate (the sole trusted component) validates it before
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//!   any `Unsat` is returned.
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//! - [`oracle`] — the Z3 differential oracle (behind the `oracle` feature).
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//!
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//! [PulseEngine]: https://github.com/pulseengine
[37](https://docs.rs#37)
[38](https://docs.rs#38)pub mod aig;
[39](https://docs.rs#39)pub mod blast;
[40](https://docs.rs#40)pub mod cnf;
[41](https://docs.rs#41)pub mod eval;
[42](https://docs.rs#42)pub mod lowering;
[43](https://docs.rs#43)pub mod lrat;

# ordeal::term - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ordeal/0.4.0/ordeal/term/index.html

## Expand description

The `ordeal` term language: the closed QF_BV fragment from loom issue #246.

This module defines the **exact, closed** set of operations `ordeal` is
designed to decide. It is deliberately small: `ordeal` is not a general
SMT solver but a specialized decision procedure for the equivalence and
satisfiability queries that loom (verified WASM optimizer) and synth
(verified WASM→ARM codegen) actually emit.

[§](https://docs.rs#the-fragment-qf_bv-widths-8--32--64)The fragment (QF_BV, widths 8 / 32 / 64)

- **Bitvector ops:**- `bvadd`,- `bvsub`,- `bvmul`,- `bvudiv`,- `bvand`,- `bvor`,- `bvxor`,- `bvshl`,- `bvlshr`,- `bvashr`,- `bvrotr`,- `extract{hi,lo}`,- `concat`,- `zero_ext{by}`,- `sign_ext{by}`.
- **Boolean predicates**(what you assert / check):- `eq`,- `ne`,- `ult`,- `ule`,- `ugt`,- `uge`,- `slt`,- `sle`,- `sgt`,- `sge`, plus- `not`/- `and`/- `or`over booleans.

A query is one-shot `check-sat` expecting **UNSAT** (equivalence holds),
returning a **counterexample model** when SAT.

[§](https://docs.rs#explicitly-out-of-scope)Explicitly out of scope

Quantifiers, floating-point, `Optimize`, and incremental solving are NOT
in scope and MUST NOT be added here. Adding an operation outside this set
silently widens the trusted fragment — do not do it.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Sort](https://docs.rs/struct.Sort.html)
- A bitvector sort, parameterized by bit width.

---

# ordeal::lowering - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ordeal/0.4.0/ordeal/lowering/index.html

## Expand description

Derived-op lowering helpers (DES-018 / TR-015).

synth-verify emits a handful of bitvector operations that the closed core
fragment ([ crate::term](https://docs.rs/term/index.html), loom #246) deliberately omits:

`bvnot`, `bvneg`,
`bvrotl`, `bvurem`, `bvsdiv`, and `bvsrem`. Rather than widen the closed set
(each new [variant would need its own proven bit-blasting rule), this module provides them as](https://docs.rs/term/enum.BvTerm.html)

`BvTerm`**derived-term constructors**: pure functions that build a

[out of the operations the core already decides.](https://docs.rs/term/enum.BvTerm.html)

`BvTerm`[§](https://docs.rs#trust)Trust

These are ordinary term builders — they are **not** new blast rules and add
nothing to the trusted base. Every `Unsat` a consumer derives from a lowered
term is still gated by the verified LRAT checker; the derived forms
themselves remain untrusted. What makes them *blessed* is that issue #29
validated these exact constructions 8-bit-exhaustively against Z3, and
[ UV-017](https://docs.rs/artifacts/field-asks.yaml) re-checks each against Z3’s
native operator (widths 8/32/64, including the division-by-zero and
signed-boundary edges) so consumers do not have to re-derive them.

[§](https://docs.rs#the-chosen-forms-all-match-smt-lib-qf_bv--z3-semantics)The chosen forms (all match SMT-LIB QF_BV / Z3 semantics)

- `bvnot x = x xor 1..1`
- `bvneg x = 0 - x`
- `bvrotl a b = rotr(a, 0 - b)`— exact for power-of-two widths (see- `bvrotl`
- `bvurem a b = a - (a udiv b) * b`— exact including- `b = 0`(SMT-LIB’s- `bvurem`by zero returns- `a`, and this form yields- `a`there too).
- `bvsdiv a b`— the SMT-LIB sign-mask construction over- `bvudiv`.
- `bvsrem a b = a - bvsdiv(a, b) * b`— exact including- `b = 0`and the- `INT_MIN / -1`overflow edge.

Widths are accepted in `1..=128`; the operands of each binary helper must
already share the given width (this module does not sort-check — build
well-sorted terms and validate with [ crate::eval::bv_sort](https://docs.rs/eval/fn.bv_sort.html)).

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [bvneg](https://docs.rs/fn.bvneg.html)
- Two’s-complement negation (`bvneg`):`0 - x`.
- [bvnot](https://docs.rs/fn.bvnot.html)
- Bitwise NOT (`bvnot`):`x xor 1..1`.
- [bvrotl](https://docs.rs/fn.bvrotl.html)
- Rotate-left (`bvrotl`) by a variable amount:`rotr(a, 0 - b)`.
- [bvsdiv](https://docs.rs/fn.bvsdiv.html)
- Signed division (`bvsdiv`) via the SMT-LIB sign-mask construction over`bvudiv`.
- [bvsrem](https://docs.rs/fn.bvsrem.html)
- Signed remainder (`bvsrem`, sign follows the dividend):`a - bvsdiv(a,b)*b`.
- [bvurem](https://docs.rs/fn.bvurem.html)
- Unsigned remainder (`bvurem`):`a - (a udiv b) * b`.
- [mask](https://docs.rs/fn.mask.html)
- The all-ones mask for a `width`-bit value (`2^width - 1`).

# ordeal::solver - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ordeal/0.4.0/ordeal/solver/index.html

## Expand description

The one-shot solver interface and the P1 pipeline dispatcher (DES-012).

Callers (loom, synth) build a conjunction of asserted [ BoolTerm](https://docs.rs/term/enum.BoolTerm.html)s and call

[. The result is one of:](https://docs.rs/struct.Solver.html#method.check)

`Solver::check`- `CheckResult::Unsat`- `Certificate`
- `CheckResult::Sat`- `Model`- **self-checked**by re-evaluating it against every assertion with the concrete evaluator.
- `CheckResult::Unknown`

[§](https://docs.rs#soundness-contract-for-callers)Soundness contract for callers

`Unknown` MUST be treated **conservatively**: loom/synth must NOT apply the
optimization / accept the codegen when they receive `Unknown`. Only a
checked `Unsat` certificate authorizes a transformation.

[§](https://docs.rs#pipeline-status-p2-certificate-checked)Pipeline status (P2: certificate-checked)

`check` runs blast → AIG → Tseitin CNF → CDCL. On SAT it returns a
self-checked model. On UNSAT the LRAT certificate emitted from the CDCL
proof trace is validated by the `ordeal-lrat` checker **before** `Unsat`
is returned — an `Unsat` the checker did not accept degrades to `Unknown`
(AGENTS.md rule 1: no unchecked `Unsat`, ever). The raw engine verdict is
exposed crate-internally for the differential oracle only.

Trust status: the checker is small, dependency-free, and mutation-tested; its formal soundness proof (Rust → Lean 4 via Aeneas, TR-013) is the remaining P2 obligation and is tracked in rivet as FEAT-002.

[§](https://docs.rs#the-op-enablement-gate-p1-kill-criterion)The op-enablement gate (P1 kill criterion)

Every operation’s blasting rule ships oracle-verified (UV-005..UV-009).
If the differential oracle ever finds a disagreement, that op is added to
[`DISABLED_OPS`] and every query containing it returns `Unknown` until
the rule is fixed — the solver reverts to conservative, never guesses.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Certificate](https://docs.rs/struct.Certificate.html)
- A machine-checkable UNSAT certificate.
- [Model](https://docs.rs/struct.Model.html)
- A satisfying assignment (counterexample) for a SAT query.
- [Solver](https://docs.rs/struct.Solver.html)
- A one-shot QF_BV solver over the closed loom #246 fragment.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Check](https://docs.rs/enum.CheckResult.html)- Result
- The verdict of a one-shot `check`.
- [OpKind](https://docs.rs/enum.OpKind.html)
- Every operation in the closed fragment, for the enablement gate.

# ordeal::eval - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ordeal/0.4.0/ordeal/eval/index.html

## Expand description

Concrete evaluator for the closed QF_BV fragment — the executable SMT-LIB semantics (DES-001).

This is the **test oracle** for every bit-blasting rule (exhaustive at
width 8, randomized at 32/64) and the SAT-model self-check: a returned
model is re-evaluated here before `check` reports `Sat`.

Values are `u128` masked to the term width. Widths are arbitrary in
1..=128 *inside* a term (an `extract` produces narrow intermediates);
the 8/32/64 restriction applies to the variables loom/synth declare.

# ordeal::aig - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ordeal/0.4.0/ordeal/aig/index.html

## Expand description

And-Inverter Graph with structural hashing and constant folding (DES-002).

AIGER literal convention: a [ Lit](https://docs.rs/struct.Lit.html) is

`variable << 1 | complement`.
Variable 0 is the constant, so `Lit(0)` is FALSE and `Lit(1)` is TRUE.
Inputs and AND nodes occupy consecutive variable indices in one arena.The [ Aig::and](https://docs.rs/struct.Aig.html#method.and) constructor folds constants (

`x&0=0`, `x&1=x`, `x&x=x`,
`x&!x=0`) and structurally hashes operand-normalized pairs, so common
subexpressions collapse before the CNF stage ever sees them.## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

# ordeal::blast - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ordeal/0.4.0/ordeal/blast/index.html

## Expand description

Bit-blasting rules: each QF_BV operation lowered to AIG gates (DES-005..DES-009), one module per op family.

Words are LSB-first [ Word](https://docs.rs/aig/type.Word.html)s. Every rule is verified
against the concrete evaluator (DES-001): exhaustively at width 8,
randomized at widths 32/64. A rule that has not passed its UV measure is
not enabled in the pipeline (the P1 kill criterion).

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [arith](https://docs.rs/arith/index.html)
- Add/sub and the eight ordered comparisons (DES-006).
- [bitwise](https://docs.rs/bitwise/index.html)
- Bitwise ops and (dis)equality (DES-005): bvand, bvor, bvxor, eq, ne.
- [muldiv](https://docs.rs/muldiv/index.html)
- Multiplication and unsigned division (DES-008): shift-add partial products; restoring long division with the SMT-LIB divide-by-zero case (divisor = 0 ⇒ all-ones quotient) merged via a divisor-is-zero mux.
- [shift](https://docs.rs/shift/index.html)
- Shifts and rotate (DES-007): barrel shifter with SMT-LIB out-of-range semantics; bvrotr rotates by amount mod width.
- [structural](https://docs.rs/structural/index.html)
- Structural ops (DES-009): extract, concat, zero_ext, sign_ext. Pure word plumbing — no gates.

# ordeal::sat - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ordeal/0.4.0/ordeal/sat/index.html

## Expand description

The pure-Rust CDCL SAT core (DES-004) — primary engine on every target.

Implements the classic conflict-driven clause-learning loop: two-watched- literal propagation, first-UIP conflict analysis with clause learning, VSIDS-style decision activities with phase saving, and Luby-sequence restarts (conflict-counter based — no wall clock, so the engine runs unchanged on wasm32-wasip2 and is fully deterministic). Learned clauses are never deleted, which also keeps proof-trace indices stable.

[§](https://docs.rs#proof-trace-the-p2-lrat-hook-tr-005)Proof trace (the P2 LRAT hook, TR-005)

Every learned clause is recorded as a [ LearnedStep](https://docs.rs/struct.LearnedStep.html) carrying the
antecedent clauses used in its conflict-analysis resolution. Antecedent
indices refer to the combined original+learned clause sequence: index

`i < n` is `formula.clauses[i]` exactly as passed to [(tautologies and duplicate literals included, so original indices line up one-to-one with the input), and index](https://docs.rs/struct.SatSolver.html#method.solve)

`SatSolver::solve``n + k` is the clause of the `k`-th
[, where](https://docs.rs/struct.LearnedStep.html)

`LearnedStep``n = formula.clauses.len()`.The antecedents of each step form a reverse-unit-propagation (RUP) chain:
assume the negation of every literal in `clause`, then process the
antecedents in order — each becomes unit (propagate its remaining
literal) until the last, which becomes falsified. Concretely the order is
root-level (level-0) unit reasons in assignment order, then the first-UIP
resolution reasons in trail order, then the conflicting clause last. When
the result is [ SatResult::Unsat](https://docs.rs/enum.SatResult.html#variant.Unsat) the final step’s

`clause` is empty:
that step records the derivation of the empty clause.## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Learned](https://docs.rs/struct.LearnedStep.html)- Step
- One clause-learning step of the resolution proof (see module docs for
the indexing convention and the RUP ordering of `antecedents`).
- [SatSolver](https://docs.rs/struct.SatSolver.html)
- The CDCL solver.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [SatResult](https://docs.rs/enum.SatResult.html)
- The verdict of a SAT solve.

# ordeal::lrat - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ordeal/0.4.0/ordeal/lrat/index.html

## Expand description

LRAT certificate emission from the CDCL proof trace (DES-013).

The CDCL core (DES-004) records every learned clause as a
[ LearnedStep](https://docs.rs/sat/struct.LearnedStep.html) whose antecedents already form a reverse-unit-propagation
chain, so emission is pure formatting into the textual LRAT dialect the

`ordeal-lrat` checker consumes:- the `k`-th learned step becomes addition line`n + k + 1`over`n`input clauses (ids strictly sequential, matching the checker);
- hints are the step’s antecedent indices, shifted to 1-based clause ids in their recorded RUP order;
- no deletion lines are emitted (the CDCL keeps learned clauses);
- an UNSAT trace ends with the empty-clause step, which is exactly the line that makes the checker accept.

The emitted certificate is UNTRUSTED output of an untrusted solver: the
pipeline (DES-013 wiring in `solver.rs`) returns `Unsat` only after the
checker accepts it.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [emit_](https://docs.rs/fn.emit_lrat.html)- lrat
- Format a proof trace as a textual LRAT certificate.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/ordeal/solver.rs.html#440-442)#### pub fn [check](https://docs.rs#method.check)(&self) -> [CheckResult](https://docs.rs/enum.CheckResult.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/ordeal/solver.rs.html#440-442)

#### pub fn [check](https://docs.rs#method.check)(&self) -> [CheckResult](https://docs.rs/enum.CheckResult.html)

Decide satisfiability of the conjunction of all asserted terms.

Pipeline: blast → AIG → Tseitin CNF → CDCL. `Sat` carries a model
that has been re-evaluated against every assertion (self-check).
On engine-UNSAT the LRAT certificate emitted from the proof trace is
validated by the `ordeal-lrat` checker before `Unsat` is returned —
an `Unsat` the checker did not accept is never reported (it degrades
to `Unknown`, which is always sound).

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/ordeal/solver.rs.html#457-459)#### pub fn [check_with_limit](https://docs.rs#method.check_with_limit)(&self, max_conflicts: [u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u64.html)) -> [CheckResult](https://docs.rs/enum.CheckResult.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/ordeal/solver.rs.html#457-459)

#### pub fn [check_with_limit](https://docs.rs#method.check_with_limit)(&self, max_conflicts: [u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u64.html)) -> [CheckResult](https://docs.rs/enum.CheckResult.html)

Decide satisfiability under a conflict budget (DES-019 / TR-016).

Runs the identical pipeline as [ Solver::check](https://docs.rs/struct.Solver.html#method.check) — blast → AIG →
Tseitin CNF → bounded CDCL — but caps the SAT core at

`max_conflicts`
search conflicts. On budget exhaustion the core reaches no verdict and
this returns [; on any decided verdict it behaves exactly like](https://docs.rs/enum.CheckResult.html#variant.Unknown)

`CheckResult::Unknown``check` (self-checked model on SAT, and on
engine-UNSAT the LRAT certificate is validated by `ordeal-lrat` before
`Unsat` is returned, degrading to `Unknown` on rejection).The budget bounds only completeness: the certificate gate and the
model self-check are untouched, so an exhausted budget yields `Unknown`
and never a wrong or unchecked verdict.

# ordeal::sliver - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ordeal/0.4.0/ordeal/sliver/index.html

## Expand description

The loom array/UF sliver (P3) — an extended query layer that is
**preprocessed away** into the closed QF_BV core before bit-blasting.

The core `term.rs` fragment stays closed (CLAUDE.md / loom #246): these
constructs have **no bit-blasting rule**. Instead they live in a separate
extended term language here and are eliminated by preprocessing
([ lower](https://docs.rs/fn.lower.html)) into a conjunction of plain

[assertions that the existing pipeline decides. No array/UF ops ever reach the AIG.](https://docs.rs/term/enum.BoolTerm.html)

`BoolTerm`What loom emits (ARCHITECTURE.md → “The array / UF sliver”, TR-008):

- **Non-extensional**modeling linear memory:- `Array(BV32 → BV8)`- `store`/- `select`over- **concrete consecutive offsets**only. No whole-array equality. Eliminated by- **eager read-over-write**: a- `select`on a- `store`chain reduces to a nested if-then-else over concrete index equalities down to the base array’s fresh per-index variables.
- **Uninterpreted**with- `pure_call`- **congruence**(same args ⇒ same result). Eliminated by- **Ackermannization**: each distinct call site becomes a fresh variable, plus congruence constraints- `args_i = args_j → result_i = result_j`across call sites of the same function.

Design decision (rivet DES-014): a separate `Ext*` layer rather than
widening `BvTerm`, so the core fragment’s “every op has a proven
bit-blasting rule” invariant is preserved by construction — the sliver
is sound *because* it never reaches the blaster, only the core does.

- [Sliver](https://docs.rs/struct.SliverModel.html)- Model

- [ExtBool](https://docs.rs/enum.ExtBoolTerm.html)- Term
- A boolean-sorted term in the extended language.
- [ExtBv](https://docs.rs/enum.ExtBvTerm.html)- Term
- A bitvector-sorted term in the extended (sliver) language: the closed
core plus `select`and uninterpreted`pure_call`.
- [ExtOp](https://docs.rs/enum.ExtOp.html)
- The recursive core operations lifted over `ExtBvTerm`children. (One variant per`BvTerm`operator that has bitvector children; leaves —`Const`/`Var`— use`ExtBvTerm::Core`
- [Sliver](https://docs.rs/enum.SliverError.html)- Error
- Why a sliver query is outside the supported fragment.

# ordeal-lrat 0.4.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/ordeal-lrat/0.4.0

Ordeal's LRAT certificate checker — **the sole trusted component**.

The ordeal solver is untrusted: an `Unsat` answer is believed only when
this checker has validated an LRAT certificate for it. This crate is
written to be translated to Lean 4 (via Aeneas) and formally verified, so
everything here is deliberately small, simple, and obviously correct:
no `unsafe`, no dependencies, no cleverness.

# Supported dialect: textual LRAT, **RUP-only**

**LOUD LIMITATION:** this checker supports only RUP (Reverse Unit
Propagation) addition steps. RAT steps — recognised by *negative* clause
ids in the hint list — are **rejected** with
[`CheckError::RatUnsupported`]. This is deliberate: ordeal's CDCL engine
emits RUP-only proofs, and rejecting is always sound (we may refuse a
valid certificate, we never accept an invalid one).

Accepted line forms (whitespace-separated integers, one step per line;
blank lines and lines starting with `c` are skipped as comments):

- Addition: `<id> <lit>* 0 <hint>* 0`— adds the clause`<lit>*`with id`<id>`, justified by unit propagation through the clauses named by`<hint>*`, in order.
- Deletion: `<id> d <id>* 0`— marks the named clauses dead. The leading`<id>`is informational (as emitted by drat-trim) and is not checked.

Clause ids are 1-based: original clause `i` of the input CNF (0-based)
has id `i + 1`; each addition step must then use exactly the next
sequential id (this is what ordeal emits; sparse ids are rejected).

# What "checked" means

An addition step `C` with hints `h1..hk` is verified by assuming the
negation of every literal of `C` and then unit-propagating through the
hint clauses in order: each hint must be either *falsified* (conflict —
the step is verified, so CNF ∧ ¬C is unsat, i.e. CNF ⊨ C) or *unit*
(its single unassigned literal is assigned true). Anything else —
a satisfied hint, a hint with two or more unassigned literals, running
out of hints, a dead or unknown id — rejects the certificate.

The whole certificate is accepted iff it parses in full AND some verified
addition step adds the **empty clause** (checking stops at that step;
parsed trailing steps are ignored). Parsing everything first is stricter
than strictly necessary and always sound (extra rejections only).

# Structure: parser vs kernel

The crate is split for the formal proof (issue #12): the [`kernel`]
module is the string-free checking core — the Aeneas → Lean translation
target carrying the soundness theorem — and this file is the untrusted
text parser feeding it. The CNF reaches the kernel directly, so parser
bugs cannot manufacture an acceptance (see `kernel` docs).

---

[154](https://docs.rs#154)            }

[157](https://docs.rs#157)                    f,
[158](https://docs.rs#158)                    "line {line}: RAT step (negative hint) — this checker is RUP-only"
[159](https://docs.rs#159)                )
[160](https://docs.rs#160)            }
[161](https://docs.rs#161)            CheckError::HintNotUnit { line, hint } => {
[162](https://docs.rs#162)                write!(
[163](https://docs.rs#163)                    f,
[164](https://docs.rs#164)                    "line {line}: hint clause {hint} is neither unit nor falsified"
[165](https://docs.rs#165)                )
[166](https://docs.rs#166)            }
[167](https://docs.rs#167)            CheckError::HintsExhausted { line } => {
[168](https://docs.rs#168)                write!(
[169](https://docs.rs#169)                    f,
[170](https://docs.rs#170)                    "line {line}: hints exhausted without reaching a conflict"
[171](https://docs.rs#171)                )
[172](https://docs.rs#172)            }
[173](https://docs.rs#173)            CheckError::NoEmptyClause => {
[174](https://docs.rs#174)                write!(f, "certificate contains no verified empty-clause addition")
[175](https://docs.rs#175)            }
[176](https://docs.rs#176)        }
[177](https://docs.rs#177)    }
[178](https://docs.rs#178)}
[179](https://docs.rs#179)
[180](https://docs.rs#180)impl std::error::Error for CheckError {}
[181](https://docs.rs#181)
[182](https://docs.rs#182)pub mod kernel;
[183](https://docs.rs#183)
[184](https://docs.rs#184)use kernel::{CoreError, Step};
[185](https://docs.rs#185)
[186](https://docs.rs#186)/// Map a kernel rejection back onto certificate line numbers.
[187](https://docs.rs#187)///
[188](https://docs.rs#188)/// `lines[step]` is the 1-based certificate line the 0-based kernel step
[189](https://docs.rs#189)/// index came from.
[190](https://docs.rs#190)fn lift(err: CoreError, lines: &[usize]) -> CheckError {
[191](https://docs.rs#191)    let at = |step: usize| lines.get(step).copied().unwrap_or(0);
[192](https://docs.rs#192)    match err {
[193](https://docs.rs#193)        CoreError::InvalidCnfLiteral { clause_index } => {
[194](https://docs.rs#194)            CheckError::InvalidCnfLiteral { clause_index }
[195](https://docs.rs#195)        }
[196](https://docs.rs#196)        // Unreachable through `check` (parse_literal rejects 0 / i32::MIN
[197](https://docs.rs#197)        // before any Step is built), but the kernel validates independently
[198](https://docs.rs#198)        // and `lift` stays total.
[199](https://docs.rs#199)        CoreError::InvalidStepLiteral { step } => CheckError::Parse {
[200](https://docs.rs#200)            line: at(step),
[201](https://docs.rs#201)            message: "step clause contains an invalid literal".to_string(),
[202](https://docs.rs#202)        },
[203](https://docs.rs#203)        CoreError::NonSequentialId {
[204](https://docs.rs#204)            step,
[205](https://docs.rs#205)            expected,
[206](https://docs.rs#206)            found,
[207](https://docs.rs#207)        } => CheckError::NonSequentialId {
[208](https://docs.rs#208)            line: at(step),
[209](https://docs.rs#209)            expected,
[210](https://docs.rs#210)            found,
[211](https://docs.rs#211)        },
[212](https://docs.rs#212)        CoreError::UnknownId { step, id } => CheckError::UnknownId { line: at(step), id },
[213](https://docs.rs#213)        CoreError::DeletedId { step, id } => CheckError::DeletedId { line: at(step), id },
[214](https://docs.rs#214)        CoreError::HintNotUnit { step, hint } => CheckError::HintNotUnit {
[215](https://docs.rs#215)            line: at(step),
[216](https://docs.rs#216)            hint,
[217](https://docs.rs#217)        },
[218](https://docs.rs#218)        CoreError::HintsExhausted { step } => CheckError::HintsExhausted { line: at(step) },
[219](https://docs.rs#219)        CoreError::NoEmptyClause => CheckError::NoEmptyClause,
[220](https://docs.rs#220)    }
[221](https://docs.rs#221)}
[222](https://docs.rs#222)
[223](https://docs.rs#223)/// Parse one whitespace token as a clause id (a positive integer).
[224](https://docs.rs#224)fn parse_id(token: &str, line: usize) -> Result<usize, CheckError> {
[225](https://docs.rs#225)    match token.parse::<usize>() {
[226](https://docs.rs#226)        Ok(id) if id >= 1 => Ok(id),
[227](https://docs.rs#227)        _ => Err(CheckError::Parse {
[228](https://docs.rs#228)            line,
[229](https://docs.rs#229)            message: format!("expected a positive clause id, found {token:?}"),
[230](https://docs.rs#230)        }),
[231](https://docs.rs#231)    }
[232](https://docs.rs#232)}
[233](https://docs.rs#233)
[234](https://docs.rs#234)/// Parse one whitespace token as a DIMACS literal (nonzero, negatable i32).
[235](https://docs.rs#235)fn parse_literal(token: &str, line: usize) -> Result<i32, CheckError> {
[236](https://docs.rs#236)    match token.parse::<i32>() {
[237](https://docs.rs#237)        // `i32::MIN` is rejected because `-lit` must not overflow.
[238](https://docs.rs#238)        Ok(lit) if lit != 0 && lit != i32::MIN => Ok(lit),
[239](https://docs.rs#239)        _ => Err(CheckError::Parse {
[240](https://docs.rs#240)            line,
[241](https://docs.rs#241)            message: format!("expected a nonzero literal, found {token:?}"),
[242](https://docs.rs#242)        }),
[243](https://docs.rs#243)    }
[244](https://docs.rs#244)}
[245](https://docs.rs#245)
[246](https://docs.rs#246)/// Parse a deletion line body (the tokens after `<id> d`): a list of clause
[247](https://docs.rs#247)/// ids terminated by `0`. Liveness of the ids is the kernel's concern.
[248](https://docs.rs#248)fn parse_deletion(tokens: &[&str], line: usize) -> Result<Vec<usize>, CheckError> {
[249](https://docs.rs#249)    let mut tokens = tokens.iter();
[250](https://docs.rs#250)    let mut ids: Vec<usize> = Vec::new();
[251](https://docs.rs#251)    loop {
[252](https://docs.rs#252)        let Some(token) = tokens.next() else {
[253](https://docs.rs#253)            return Err(CheckError::Parse {
[254](https://docs.rs#254)                line,
[255](https://docs.rs#255)                message: "deletion line missing terminating 0".to_string(),
[256](https://docs.rs#256)            });
[257](https://docs.rs#257)        };
[258](https://docs.rs#258)        if *token == "0" {
[259](https://docs.rs#259)            break;
[260](https://docs.rs#260)        }
[261](https://docs.rs#261)        ids.push(parse_id(token, line)?);
[262](https://docs.rs#262)    }
[263](https://docs.rs#263)    if tokens.next().is_some() {
[264](https://docs.rs#264)        return Err(CheckError::Parse {
[265](https://docs.rs#265)            line,
[266](https://docs.rs#266)            message: "trailing tokens after deletion terminator".to_string(),
[267](https://docs.rs#267)        });
[268](https://docs.rs#268)    }
[269](https://docs.rs#269)    Ok(ids)
[270](https://docs.rs#270)}
[271](https://docs.rs#271)
[272](https://docs.rs#272)/// Parse an addition line body (the tokens after `<id>`): the new clause's
[273](https://docs.rs#273)/// literals terminated by `0`, then the RUP hints terminated by `0`.
[274](https://docs.rs#274)/// Sequential-id and RUP checking are the kernel's concern; RAT detection
[275](https://docs.rs#275)/// (a negative hint id) happens here because sign lives in the text.
[276](https://docs.rs#276)fn parse_addition(tokens: &[&str], line: usize) -> Result<(Vec<i32>, Vec<usize>), CheckError> {
[277](https://docs.rs#277)    let mut tokens = tokens.iter();
[278](https://docs.rs#278)
[279](https://docs.rs#279)    // The new clause: literals up to the first `0`.
[280](https://docs.rs#280)    let mut new_clause: Vec<i32> = Vec::new();
[281](https://docs.rs#281)    loop {
[282](https://docs.rs#282)        let Some(token) = tokens.next() else {
[283](https://docs.rs#283)            return Err(CheckError::Parse {
[284](https://docs.rs#284)                line,
[285](https://docs.rs#285)                message: "missing terminating 0 after clause literals".to_string(),
[286](https://docs.rs#286)            });
[287](https://docs.rs#287)        };
[288](https://docs.rs#288)        if *token == "0" {
[289](https://docs.rs#289)            break;
[290](https://docs.rs#290)        }
[291](https://docs.rs#291)        new_clause.push(parse_literal(token, line)?);
[292](https://docs.rs#292)    }
[293](https://docs.rs#293)
[294](https://docs.rs#294)    // The hints: clause ids up to the second `0`. A negative id marks a RAT
[295](https://docs.rs#295)    // step, which this RUP-only checker rejects (see the crate docs).
[296](https://docs.rs#296)    let mut hints: Vec<usize> = Vec::new();
[297](https://docs.rs#297)    loop {
[298](https://docs.rs#298)        let Some(token) = tokens.next() else {
[299](https://docs.rs#299)            return Err(CheckError::Parse {
[300](https://docs.rs#300)                line,
[301](https://docs.rs#301)                message: "missing terminating 0 after hints".to_string(),
[302](https://docs.rs#302)            });
[303](https://docs.rs#303)        };
[304](https://docs.rs#304)        if *token == "0" {
[305](https://docs.rs#305)            break;
[306](https://docs.rs#306)        }
[307](https://docs.rs#307)        if token.starts_with('-') {
[308](https://docs.rs#308)            return Err(CheckError::RatUnsupported { line });
[309](https://docs.rs#309)        }
[310](https://docs.rs#310)        hints.push(parse_id(token, line)?);
[311](https://docs.rs#311)    }
[312](https://docs.rs#312)    if tokens.next().is_some() {
[313](https://docs.rs#313)        return Err(CheckError::Parse {
[314](https://docs.rs#314)            line,
[315](https://docs.rs#315)            message: "trailing tokens after hint terminator".to_string(),
[316](https://docs.rs#316)        });
[317](https://docs.rs#317)    }
[318](https://docs.rs#318)    Ok((new_clause, hints))
[319](https://docs.rs#319)}
[320](https://docs.rs#320)
[321](https://docs.rs#321)/// Parse a full certificate into kernel steps plus, per step, the 1-based
[322](https://docs.rs#322)/// certificate line it came from (for error reporting).
[323](https://docs.rs#323)fn parse_certificate(certificate: &str) -> Result<(Vec<Step>, Vec<usize>), CheckError> {
[324](https://docs.rs#324)    let mut steps: Vec<Step> = Vec::new();
[325](https://docs.rs#325)    let mut lines: Vec<usize> = Vec::new();
[326](https://docs.rs#326)    for (line_index, raw_line) in certificate.lines().enumerate() {
[327](https://docs.rs#327)        let line = line_index + 1; // 1-based, for error reporting
[328](https://docs.rs#328)        let tokens: Vec<&str> = raw_line.split_whitespace().collect();
[329](https://docs.rs#329)        match tokens.first() {
[330](https://docs.rs#330)            None => continue,                                  // blank line
[331](https://docs.rs#331)            Some(first) if first.starts_with('c') => continue, // comment
[332](https://docs.rs#332)            Some(first) => {
[333](https://docs.rs#333)                let id = parse_id(first, line)?;
[334](https://docs.rs#334)                let step = if tokens.get(1) == Some(&"d") {
[335](https://docs.rs#335)                    // The leading id of a deletion line is informational.
[336](https://docs.rs#336)                    Step::Delete {
[337](https://docs.rs#337)                        ids: parse_deletion(&tokens[2..], line)?,
[338](https://docs.rs#338)                    }
[339](https://docs.rs#339)                } else {
[340](https://docs.rs#340)                    let (clause, hints) = parse_addition(&tokens[1..], line)?;
[341](https://docs.rs#341)                    Step::Add { id, clause, hints }
[342](https://docs.rs#342)                };
[343](https://docs.rs#343)                steps.push(step);
[344](https://docs.rs#344)                lines.push(line);
[345](https://docs.rs#345)            }
[346](https://docs.rs#346)        }
[347](https://docs.rs#347)    }
[348](https://docs.rs#348)    Ok((steps, lines))
[349](https://docs.rs#349)}
[350](https://docs.rs#350)
[351](https://docs.rs#351)/// Check a textual LRAT `certificate` against the input `cnf`.
[352](https://docs.rs#352)///
[353](https://docs.rs#353)/// `cnf` is the clause list in DIMACS literal convention (variable `v` is
[354](https://docs.rs#354)/// the literal `v`, its negation `-v`; `0` is not a literal). Clause ids in
[355](https://docs.rs#355)/// the certificate are 1-based: original clause `i` (0-based) has id
[356](https://docs.rs#356)/// `i + 1`, and added clauses take sequential ids after that.
[357](https://docs.rs#357)///
[358](https://docs.rs#358)/// Returns `Ok(())` iff the certificate contains a verified addition of the
[359](https://docs.rs#359)/// **empty clause**, which proves the CNF unsatisfiable. Any other outcome —
[360](https://docs.rs#360)/// including certificates that are merely *not understood* (parse errors,
[361](https://docs.rs#361)/// RAT steps) — is a rejection. Rejection never means "satisfiable"; it
[362](https://docs.rs#362)/// only means "not proven unsatisfiable by this certificate".
[363](https://docs.rs#363)pub fn check(cnf: &[Vec<i32>], certificate: &str) -> Result<(), CheckError> {
[364](https://docs.rs#364)    // Parse the whole certificate first (the untrusted, string-facing half),
[365](https://docs.rs#365)    // then run the string-free kernel (the Aeneas → Lean target) over the
[366](https://docs.rs#366)    // parsed steps. Soundness never depends on the parser: the CNF reaches
[367](https://docs.rs#367)    // the kernel directly, so a parser bug can only change WHICH steps get
[368](https://docs.rs#368)    // checked — every accepted certificate was still kernel-verified against
[369](https://docs.rs#369)    // the real CNF. See `kernel` module docs and issue #12.
[370](https://docs.rs#370)    let (steps, lines) = parse_certificate(certificate)?;
[371](https://docs.rs#371)    kernel::check_steps(cnf, &steps).map_err(|e| lift(e, &lines))
[372](https://docs.rs#372)}
[373](https://docs.rs#373)
[374](https://docs.rs#374)#[cfg(test)]
[375](https://docs.rs#375)mod tests {
[376](https://docs.rs#376)    use super::*;
[377](https://docs.rs#377)
[378](https://docs.rs#378)    /// The 2-clause contradiction: (x1) ∧ (¬x1).
[379](https://docs.rs#379)    fn tiny_cnf() -> Vec<Vec<i32>> {
[380](https://docs.rs#380)        vec![vec![1], vec![-1]]
[381](https://docs.rs#381)    }
[382](https://docs.rs#382)
[383](https://docs.rs#383)    /// The 4-clause full contradiction over x1, x2:
[384](https://docs.rs#384)    /// ids 1..=4 are [1,2], [-1,2], [1,-2], [-1,-2].
[385](https://docs.rs#385)    fn quad_cnf() -> Vec<Vec<i32>> {
[386](https://docs.rs#386)        vec![vec![1, 2], vec![-1, 2], vec![1, -2], vec![-1, -2]]
[387](https://docs.rs#387)    }
[388](https://docs.rs#388)
[389](https://docs.rs#389)    // ── Hand-verified ACCEPT cases (UV-011) ─────────────────────────────
[390](https://docs.rs#390)
[391](https://docs.rs#391)    /// (a) Empty clause directly from the two unit clauses: assuming
[392](https://docs.rs#392)    /// nothing, hint 1 = [1] is unit (assign x1), hint 2 = [-1] is
[393](https://docs.rs#393)    /// falsified — conflict, step verified.
[394](https://docs.rs#394)    #[test]
[395](https://docs.rs#395)    fn accepts_two_unit_contradiction() {
[396](https://docs.rs#396)        assert_eq!(check(&tiny_cnf(), "3 0 1 2 0"), Ok(()));
[397](https://docs.rs#397)    }
[398](https://docs.rs#398)
[399](https://docs.rs#399)    /// (b) Hand-derived RUP chain: first add [2] (assume ¬x2; hint 1 =
[400](https://docs.rs#400)    /// [1,2] is unit on x1; hint 2 = [-1,2] is falsified). Then the empty
[401](https://docs.rs#401)    /// clause (hint 5 = [2] is unit on x2; hint 3 = [1,-2] is unit on x1;
[402](https://docs.rs#402)    /// hint 4 = [-1,-2] is falsified).
[403](https://docs.rs#403)    #[test]
[404](https://docs.rs#404)    fn accepts_quad_cnf_rup_chain() {
[405](https://docs.rs#405)        let cert = "5 2 0 1 2 0\n6 0 5 3 4 0";
[406](https://docs.rs#406)        assert_eq!(check(&quad_cnf(), cert), Ok(()));
[407](https://docs.rs#407)    }
[408](https://docs.rs#408)
[409](https://docs.rs#409)    /// (c) Same proof with a deletion line in the middle: clauses 1 and 2
[410](https://docs.rs#410)    /// are dead by the final step, which only uses 5, 3, 4.
[411](https://docs.rs#411)    #[test]
[412](https://docs.rs#412)    fn accepts_proof_with_deletion() {
[413](https://docs.rs#413)        let cert = "5 2 0 1 2 0\n5 d 1 2 0\n6 0 5 3 4 0";
[414](https://docs.rs#414)        assert_eq!(check(&quad_cnf(), cert), Ok(()));
[415](https://docs.rs#415)    }
[416](https://docs.rs#416)
[417](https://docs.rs#417)    // ── Mutation REJECT cases (UV-011) ──────────────────────────────────
[418](https://docs.rs#418)
[419](https://docs.rs#419)    /// Dropped hint: without hint 4 the final chain propagates but never

[421](https://docs.rs#421)    #[test]

[429](https://docs.rs#429)

[511](https://docs.rs#511)    // ── Dependency-graph guard (UV-011) ─────────────────────────────────
[512](https://docs.rs#512)
[513](https://docs.rs#513)    /// TRUST BOUNDARY GUARD: this crate must depend on nothing — in
[514](https://docs.rs#514)    /// particular not on the untrusted `ordeal` crate. The fact that this
[515](https://docs.rs#515)    /// test compiled at all already proves the crate builds without

Why a certificate was rejected (or could not even be read).

Every variant carries the 1-based certificate line number where checking
stopped, except [ CheckError::NoEmptyClause](https://docs.rs/enum.CheckError.html#variant.NoEmptyClause) (a property of the whole
certificate) and

[(a property of the input CNF).](https://docs.rs/enum.CheckError.html#variant.InvalidCnfLiteral)

`CheckError::InvalidCnfLiteral`## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.InvalidCnfLiteral)

### InvalidCnfLiteral

The input CNF itself is malformed: a clause contains the literal `0`
(or `i32::MIN`, whose negation would overflow).

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Parse)

### Parse

A certificate line could not be parsed.

#### Fields

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.NonSequentialId)

### NonSequentialId

An addition step did not use the next sequential clause id.

#### Fields

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.UnknownId)

### UnknownId

A hint or deletion referenced an id that was never assigned.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.DeletedId)

### DeletedId

A hint or deletion referenced a clause that was already deleted.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.RatUnsupported)

### RatUnsupported

A negative hint id was found: a RAT step, which this RUP-only checker does not support (see the crate docs).

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.HintNotUnit)

### HintNotUnit

A hint clause was neither unit nor falsified under the current assignment (it was satisfied, or had two or more unassigned literals), so unit propagation cannot use it.

#### Fields

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.HintsExhausted)

### HintsExhausted

The hint list ended before unit propagation reached a conflict, so the addition step is not justified.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.NoEmptyClause)

### NoEmptyClause

The certificate ended without a verified addition of the empty clause, so unsatisfiability was not established.

# ordeal_lrat::kernel - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ordeal-lrat/0.4.0/ordeal_lrat/kernel/index.html

## Expand description

The string-free checking core — **the Aeneas → Lean translation target**.

Everything semantic lives here, over already-parsed data: no `&str`, no
`String`, no formatting, no I/O. The soundness theorem (issue #12) is
stated about [ check_steps](https://docs.rs/fn.check_steps.html):

If

`check_steps(cnf, steps)`returns`Ok(())`, then`cnf`is unsatisfiable.

The text parser (in `lib.rs`) is **outside** this trusted core, and that
is sound by construction: the CNF reaches [ check_steps](https://docs.rs/fn.check_steps.html) directly (never
through the parser), so a buggy parser can only produce a

*different*step list — which still has to check against the real CNF — or reject. It can never manufacture an acceptance the core would not itself verify.

[§](https://docs.rs#style-constraints-aeneas)Style constraints (Aeneas)

This module is written in the fragment Aeneas translates cleanly today:
index-based `while` loops instead of iterators/closures, no early
`return` inside nested loops (every inner loop is its own function), no
slice patterns, and no std methods beyond `Vec::{new, push, len}` and
indexing. Keep it that way — a “cleanup” that reintroduces iterator
sugar breaks the translation.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Core](https://docs.rs/enum.CoreError.html)- Error
- Why the core rejected. Data-only (no strings) so the Lean model stays
simple; `step`is the 0-based index into the step list (the parser maps it back to a certificate line for reporting).
- [Step](https://docs.rs/enum.Step.html)
- One already-parsed certificate step.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [check_](https://docs.rs/fn.check_steps.html)- steps
- Check a parsed step list against the input CNF.

# check in ordeal_lrat - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ordeal-lrat/0.4.0/ordeal_lrat/fn.check.html

## Expand description

Check a textual LRAT `certificate` against the input `cnf`.

`cnf` is the clause list in DIMACS literal convention (variable `v` is
the literal `v`, its negation `-v`; `0` is not a literal). Clause ids in
the certificate are 1-based: original clause `i` (0-based) has id
`i + 1`, and added clauses take sequential ids after that.

Returns `Ok(())` iff the certificate contains a verified addition of the
**empty clause**, which proves the CNF unsatisfiable. Any other outcome —
including certificates that are merely *not understood* (parse errors,
RAT steps) — is a rejection. Rejection never means “satisfiable”; it
only means “not proven unsatisfiable by this certificate”.

# async_trait - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/async-trait/^0.1/

## Expand description

#### Type erasure for async trait methods

The stabilization of async functions in traits in Rust 1.75 did not include
support for using traits containing async functions as `dyn Trait`. Trying
to use dyn with an async trait produces the following error:

```
error[E0038]: the trait `Trait` is not dyn compatible
 --> src/main.rs:5:22
  |
5 | pub fn make() -> Box<dyn Trait> {
  |                      ^^^^^^^^^ `Trait` is not dyn compatible
  |
note: for a trait to be dyn compatible it needs to allow building a vtable
      for more information, visit <https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility>
 --> src/main.rs:2:14
  |
1 | pub trait Trait {
  |           ----- this trait is not dyn compatible...
2 |     async fn f(&self);
  |              ^ ...because method `f` is `async`
  = help: consider moving `f` to another trait
```
This crate provides an attribute macro to make async fn in traits work with dyn traits.

Please refer to [ why async fn in traits are hard](https://smallcultfollowing.com/babysteps/blog/2019/10/26/async-fn-in-traits-are-hard/) for a deeper
analysis of how this implementation differs from what the compiler and
language deliver natively.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

This example implements the core of a highly effective advertising platform using async fn in a trait.

The only thing to notice here is that we write an `#[async_trait]` macro on
top of traits and trait impls that contain async fn, and then they work. We
get to have `Vec<Box<dyn Advertisement + Sync>>` or `&[&dyn Advertisement]`,
for example.

```
use async_trait::async_trait;
#[async_trait]
trait Advertisement {
    async fn run(&self);
}
struct Modal;
#[async_trait]
impl Advertisement for Modal {
    async fn run(&self) {
        self.render_fullscreen().await;
        for _ in 0..4u16 {
            remind_user_to_join_mailing_list().await;
        }
        self.hide_for_now().await;
    }
}
struct AutoplayingVideo {
    media_url: String,
}
#[async_trait]
impl Advertisement for AutoplayingVideo {
    async fn run(&self) {
        let stream = connect(&self.media_url).await;
        stream.play().await;
        // Video probably persuaded user to join our mailing list!
        Modal.run().await;
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#supported-features)Supported features

It is the intention that all features of Rust traits should work nicely with
#[async_trait], but the edge cases are numerous. Please file an issue if
you see unexpected borrow checker errors, type errors, or warnings. There is
no use of `unsafe` in the expanded code, so rest assured that if your code
compiles it can’t be that badly broken.

☑ Self by value, by reference, by mut reference, or no self;

☑ Any number of arguments, any return value;

☑ Generic type parameters and lifetime parameters;

☑ Associated types;

☑ Having async and non-async functions in the same trait;

☑ Default implementations provided by the trait;

☑ Elided lifetimes.

[§](https://docs.rs#explanation)Explanation

Async fns get transformed into methods that return `Pin<Box<dyn Future + Send + 'async_trait>>` and delegate to an async block.

For example the `impl Advertisement for AutoplayingVideo` above would be
expanded as:

```
impl Advertisement for AutoplayingVideo {
    fn run<'async_trait>(
        &'async_trait self,
    ) -> Pin<Box<dyn core::future::Future<Output = ()> + Send + 'async_trait>>
    where
        Self: Sync + 'async_trait,
    {
        Box::pin(async move {
            /* the original method body */
        })
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#non-threadsafe-futures)Non-threadsafe futures

Not all async traits need futures that are `dyn Future + Send`. To avoid
having Send and Sync bounds placed on the async trait methods, invoke the
async trait macro as `#[async_trait(?Send)]` on both the trait and the impl
blocks.

[§](https://docs.rs#elided-lifetimes)Elided lifetimes

Be aware that async fn syntax does not allow lifetime elision outside of `&`
and `&mut` references. (This is true even when not using #[async_trait].)
Lifetimes must be named or marked by the placeholder `'_`.

Fortunately the compiler is able to diagnose missing lifetimes with a good error message.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
type Elided<'a> = &'a usize;
#[async_trait]
trait Test {
    async fn test(not_okay: Elided, okay: &usize) {}
}
```
```
error[E0726]: implicit elided lifetime not allowed here
 --> src/main.rs:9:29
  |
9 |     async fn test(not_okay: Elided, okay: &usize) {}
  |                             ^^^^^^- help: indicate the anonymous lifetime: `<'_>`
```
The fix is to name the lifetime or use `'_`.

```
#[async_trait]
trait Test {
    // either
    async fn test<'e>(elided: Elided<'e>) {}
    // or
    async fn test(elided: Elided<'_>) {}
}
```

# base64 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/base64/^0.22/

## Expand description

Correct, fast, and configurable [base64](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/Base64) decoding and encoding. Base64
transports binary data efficiently in contexts where only plain text is
allowed.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

Use an [ Engine](https://docs.rs/engine/trait.Engine.html) to decode or encode base64, configured with the base64
alphabet and padding behavior best suited to your application.

[§](https://docs.rs#engine-setup)Engine setup

There is more than one way to encode a stream of bytes as “base64”.
Different applications use different encoding
[alphabets](https://docs.rs/alphabet/struct.Alphabet.html) and
[padding behaviors](https://docs.rs/engine/general_purpose/struct.GeneralPurposeConfig.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#encoding-alphabet)Encoding alphabet

Almost all base64 [alphabets](https://docs.rs/alphabet/struct.Alphabet.html) use `A-Z`, `a-z`, and
`0-9`, which gives nearly 64 characters (26 + 26 + 10 = 62), but they differ
in their choice of their final 2.

Most applications use the [standard](https://docs.rs/alphabet/constant.STANDARD.html) alphabet specified
in [RFC 4648](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc4648#section-4).  If that’s all you need, you can get started
quickly by using the pre-configured
[ STANDARD](https://docs.rs/engine/general_purpose/constant.STANDARD.html) engine, which is also available
in the

[module as shown here, if you prefer a minimal](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)

`prelude``use`
footprint.```
use base64::prelude::*;
assert_eq!(BASE64_STANDARD.decode(b"+uwgVQA=")?, b"\xFA\xEC\x20\x55\0");
assert_eq!(BASE64_STANDARD.encode(b"\xFF\xEC\x20\x55\0"), "/+wgVQA=");
```
Other common alphabets are available in the [ alphabet](https://docs.rs/alphabet/index.html) module.

[§](https://docs.rs#url-safe-alphabet)URL-safe alphabet

The standard alphabet uses `+` and `/` as its two non-alphanumeric tokens,
which cannot be safely used in URL’s without encoding them as `%2B` and
`%2F`.

To avoid that, some applications use a [“URL-safe” alphabet](https://docs.rs/alphabet/constant.URL_SAFE.html),
which uses `-` and `_` instead. To use that alternative alphabet, use the
[ URL_SAFE](https://docs.rs/engine/general_purpose/constant.URL_SAFE.html) engine. This example doesn’t
use

[to show what a more explicit](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)

`prelude``use` would look like.```
use base64::{engine::general_purpose::URL_SAFE, Engine as _};
assert_eq!(URL_SAFE.decode(b"-uwgVQA=")?, b"\xFA\xEC\x20\x55\0");
assert_eq!(URL_SAFE.encode(b"\xFF\xEC\x20\x55\0"), "_-wgVQA=");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#padding-characters)Padding characters

Each base64 character represents 6 bits (2⁶ = 64) of the original binary data, and every 3 bytes of input binary data will encode to 4 base64 characters (8 bits × 3 = 6 bits × 4 = 24 bits).

When the input is not an even multiple of 3 bytes in length, [canonical](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc4648#section-3.5)
base64 encoders insert padding characters at the end, so that the output
length is always a multiple of 4:

```
use base64::{engine::general_purpose::STANDARD, Engine as _};
assert_eq!(STANDARD.encode(b""),    "");
assert_eq!(STANDARD.encode(b"f"),   "Zg==");
assert_eq!(STANDARD.encode(b"fo"),  "Zm8=");
assert_eq!(STANDARD.encode(b"foo"), "Zm9v");
```
Canonical encoding ensures that base64 encodings will be exactly the same,
byte-for-byte, regardless of input length. But the `=` padding characters
aren’t necessary for decoding, and they may be omitted by using a
[ NO_PAD](https://docs.rs/engine/general_purpose/constant.NO_PAD.html) configuration:

```
use base64::{engine::general_purpose::STANDARD_NO_PAD, Engine as _};
assert_eq!(STANDARD_NO_PAD.encode(b""),    "");
assert_eq!(STANDARD_NO_PAD.encode(b"f"),   "Zg");
assert_eq!(STANDARD_NO_PAD.encode(b"fo"),  "Zm8");
assert_eq!(STANDARD_NO_PAD.encode(b"foo"), "Zm9v");
```
The pre-configured `NO_PAD` engines will reject inputs containing padding
`=` characters. To encode without padding and still accept padding while
decoding, create an [engine](https://docs.rs/engine/general_purpose/struct.GeneralPurpose.html) with
that [padding mode](https://docs.rs/engine/enum.DecodePaddingMode.html).

`assert_eq!(STANDARD_NO_PAD.decode(b"Zm8="), Err(base64::DecodeError::InvalidPadding));`[§](https://docs.rs#further-customization)Further customization

Decoding and encoding behavior can be customized by creating an
[engine](https://docs.rs/engine/general_purpose/struct.GeneralPurpose.html) with an [alphabet](https://docs.rs/alphabet/struct.Alphabet.html) and
[padding configuration](https://docs.rs/engine/general_purpose/struct.GeneralPurposeConfig.html):

```
use base64::{engine, alphabet, Engine as _};
// bizarro-world base64: +/ as the first symbols instead of the last
let alphabet =
    alphabet::Alphabet::new("+/ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz0123456789")
    .unwrap();
// a very weird config that encodes with padding but requires no padding when decoding...?
let crazy_config = engine::GeneralPurposeConfig::new()
    .with_decode_allow_trailing_bits(true)
    .with_encode_padding(true)
    .with_decode_padding_mode(engine::DecodePaddingMode::RequireNone);
let crazy_engine = engine::GeneralPurpose::new(&alphabet, crazy_config);
let encoded = crazy_engine.encode(b"abc 123");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#memory-allocation)Memory allocation

The [decode](https://docs.rs/engine/trait.Engine.html#method.decode) and [encode](https://docs.rs/engine/trait.Engine.html#method.encode) engine methods
allocate memory for their results – `decode` returns a `Vec<u8>` and
`encode` returns a `String`. To instead decode or encode into a buffer that
you allocated, use one of the alternative methods:

[§](https://docs.rs#decoding)Decoding

| Method | Output | Allocates memory |
|---|---|---|
| `Engine::decode` | returns a new `Vec<u8>` | always |
| `Engine::decode_vec` | appends to provided `Vec<u8>` | if `Vec`lacks capacity |
| `Engine::decode_slice` | writes to provided `&[u8]` | never |

[§](https://docs.rs#encoding)Encoding

| Method | Output | Allocates memory |
|---|---|---|
| `Engine::encode` | returns a new `String` | always |
| `Engine::encode_string` | appends to provided `String` | if `String`lacks capacity |
| `Engine::encode_slice` | writes to provided `&[u8]` | never |

[§](https://docs.rs#input-and-output)Input and output

The `base64` crate can [decode](https://docs.rs/engine/trait.Engine.html#method.decode) and
[encode](https://docs.rs/engine/trait.Engine.html#method.encode) values in memory, or
[ DecoderReader](https://docs.rs/read/struct.DecoderReader.html) and

[provide streaming decoding and encoding for any](https://docs.rs/write/struct.EncoderWriter.html)

`EncoderWriter`[readable](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/trait.Read.html)or

[writable](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/trait.Write.html)byte stream.

[§](https://docs.rs#decoding-1)Decoding

```
use base64::{engine::general_purpose::STANDARD, read::DecoderReader};
let mut input = io::stdin();
let mut decoder = DecoderReader::new(&mut input, &STANDARD);
io::copy(&mut decoder, &mut io::stdout())?;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#encoding-1)Encoding

```
use base64::{engine::general_purpose::STANDARD, write::EncoderWriter};
let mut output = io::stdout();
let mut encoder = EncoderWriter::new(&mut output, &STANDARD);
io::copy(&mut io::stdin(), &mut encoder)?;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#display)Display

If you only need a base64 representation for implementing the
[ Display](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Display.html) trait, use

[:](https://docs.rs/display/struct.Base64Display.html)

`Base64Display````
use base64::{display::Base64Display, engine::general_purpose::STANDARD};
let value = Base64Display::new(b"\0\x01\x02\x03", &STANDARD);
assert_eq!("base64: AAECAw==", format!("base64: {}", value));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

If length calculations result in overflowing `usize`, a panic will result.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

# ciborium - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ciborium/^0.2/

## Expand description

Welcome to Ciborium!

Ciborium contains CBOR serialization and deserialization implementations for serde.

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

You’re probably looking for [ from_reader()](https://docs.rs/fn.from_reader.html)
and

[, which are the main functions. Note that byte slices are also readers and writers and can be passed to these functions just as streams can.](https://docs.rs/fn.into_writer.html)

`into_writer()`For dynamic CBOR value creation/inspection, see [ Value](https://docs.rs/enum.Value.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#design-decisions)Design Decisions

[§](https://docs.rs#always-serialize-numeric-values-to-the-smallest-size)Always Serialize Numeric Values to the Smallest Size

Although the CBOR specification has differing numeric widths, this is only
a form of compression on the wire and is not intended to directly
represent an “integer width” or “float width.” Therefore, ciborium always
serializes numbers to the smallest possible lossless encoding. For example,
we serialize `1u128` as a single byte (`01`). Likewise, we will also freely
decode that single byte into a `u128`.

While there is some minor performance cost for this, there are several reasons for this choice. First, the specification seems to imply it by using a separate bit for the sign. Second, the specification requires that implementations handle leading zeroes; a liberal reading of which implies a requirement for lossless coercion. Third, dynamic languages like Python have no notion of “integer width,” making this is a practical choice for maximizing wire compatibility with those languages.

This coercion is **always** lossless. For floats, this implies that we
only coerce to a smaller size if coercion back to the original size has
the same raw bits as the original.

[§](https://docs.rs#compatibility-with-other-implementations)Compatibility with Other Implementations

The ciborium project follows the [Robustness Principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robustness_principle).
Therefore, we aim to be liberal in what we accept. This implies that we
aim to be wire-compatible with other implementations in decoding, but
not necessarily encoding.

One notable example of this is that `serde_cbor` uses fixed-width encoding
of numbers and doesn’t losslessly coerce. This implies that `ciborium` will
successfully decode `serde_cbor` encodings, but the opposite may not be the
case.

[§](https://docs.rs#representing-map-as-a-sequence-of-values)Representing Map as a Sequence of Values

Other serde parsers have generally taken the route of using `BTreeMap` or
`HashMap` to implement their encoding’s underlying `Map` type. This crate
chooses to represent the `Map` type using `Vec<(Value, Value)>` instead.

This decision was made because this type preserves the order of the pairs
on the wire. Further, for those that need the properties of `BTreeMap` or
`HashMap`, you can simply `collect()` the values into the respective type.
This provides maximum flexibility.

[§](https://docs.rs#low-level-library)Low-level Library

The ciborium crate has the beginnings of a low-level library in the
(private) `basic` module. We may extend this to be more robust and expose
it for application consumption once we have it in a good state. If you’d
like to collaborate with us on that, please contact us. Alternatively,
we might fork this code into a separate crate with no serde dependency.

[§](https://docs.rs#internal-types)Internal Types

The ciborium crate contains a number of internal types that implement useful serde traits. While these are not currently exposed, we might choose to expose them in the future if there is demand. Generally, this crate takes a conservative approach to exposing APIs to avoid breakage.

[§](https://docs.rs#packed-encoding)Packed Encoding?

Packed encoding uses numerical offsets to represent structure field names and enum variant names. This can save significant space on the wire.

While the authors of this crate like packed encoding, it should generally be avoided because it can be fragile as it exposes invariants of your Rust code to remote actors. We might consider adding this in the future. If you are interested in this, please contact us.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [de](https://docs.rs/de/index.html)
- Serde deserialization support for CBOR
- [ser](https://docs.rs/ser/index.html)
- Serde serialization support for CBOR
- [tag](https://docs.rs/tag/index.html)
- Contains helper types for dealing with CBOR tags

# ed25519_dalek - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ed25519-dalek/^2.0/

## Expand description

A Rust implementation of ed25519 key generation, signing, and verification.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

Creating an ed25519 signature on a message is simple.

First, we need to generate a `SigningKey`, which includes both public and
secret halves of an asymmetric key.  To do so, we need a cryptographically
secure pseudorandom number generator (CSPRNG). For this example, we’ll use
the operating system’s builtin PRNG:

```
// $ cargo add ed25519_dalek --features rand_core
use rand::rngs::OsRng;
use ed25519_dalek::SigningKey;
use ed25519_dalek::Signature;
let mut csprng = OsRng;
let signing_key: SigningKey = SigningKey::generate(&mut csprng);
```
We can now use this `signing_key` to sign a message:

```
use ed25519_dalek::{Signature, Signer};
let message: &[u8] = b"This is a test of the tsunami alert system.";
let signature: Signature = signing_key.sign(message);
```
As well as to verify that this is, indeed, a valid signature on
that `message`:

```
use ed25519_dalek::Verifier;
assert!(signing_key.verify(message, &signature).is_ok());
```
Anyone else, given the `public` half of the `signing_key` can also easily
verify this signature:

```
use ed25519_dalek::{VerifyingKey, Verifier};
let verifying_key: VerifyingKey = signing_key.verifying_key();
assert!(verifying_key.verify(message, &signature).is_ok());
```
[§](https://docs.rs#serialisation)Serialisation

`VerifyingKey`s, `SecretKey`s, `SigningKey`s, and `Signature`s can be serialised
into byte-arrays by calling `.to_bytes()`.  It’s perfectly acceptable and
safe to transfer and/or store those bytes.  (Of course, never transfer your
secret key to anyone else, since they will only need the public key to
verify your signatures!)

```
use ed25519_dalek::{PUBLIC_KEY_LENGTH, SECRET_KEY_LENGTH, KEYPAIR_LENGTH, SIGNATURE_LENGTH};
let verifying_key_bytes: [u8; PUBLIC_KEY_LENGTH] = signing_key.verifying_key().to_bytes();
let secret_key_bytes: [u8; SECRET_KEY_LENGTH] = signing_key.to_bytes();
let signing_key_bytes:    [u8; KEYPAIR_LENGTH]    = signing_key.to_keypair_bytes();
let signature_bytes:  [u8; SIGNATURE_LENGTH]  = signature.to_bytes();
```
And similarly, decoded from bytes with `::from_bytes()`:

```
let verifying_key: VerifyingKey = VerifyingKey::from_bytes(&verifying_key_bytes)?;
let signing_key: SigningKey = SigningKey::from_bytes(&signing_key_bytes);
let signature: Signature = Signature::try_from(&signature_bytes[..])?;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#pkcs8-key-encoding)PKCS#8 Key Encoding

PKCS#8 is a private key format with support for multiple algorithms. It can be encoded as binary (DER) or text (PEM).

You can recognize PEM-encoded PKCS#8 keys by the following:

`-----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----`To use PKCS#8, you need to enable the `pkcs8` crate feature.

The following traits can be used to decode/encode [ SigningKey](https://docs.rs/struct.SigningKey.html) and

[as PKCS#8. Note that](https://docs.rs/struct.VerifyingKey.html)

`VerifyingKey`[is re-exported from the toplevel of the crate:](https://docs.rs/pkcs8/index.html)

`pkcs8`- `pkcs8::DecodePrivateKey`
- `pkcs8::EncodePrivateKey`
- `pkcs8::DecodePublicKey`
- `pkcs8::EncodePublicKey`

[§](https://docs.rs#example-1)Example

NOTE: this requires the `pem` crate feature.

```
use ed25519_dalek::{VerifyingKey, pkcs8::DecodePublicKey};
let pem = "-----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----
MCowBQYDK2VwAyEAGb9ECWmEzf6FQbrBZ9w7lshQhqowtrbLDFw4rXAxZuE=
-----END PUBLIC KEY-----";
let verifying_key = VerifyingKey::from_public_key_pem(pem)
    .expect("invalid public key PEM");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#using-serde)Using Serde

If you prefer the bytes to be wrapped in another serialisation format, all
types additionally come with built-in [serde](https://serde.rs) support by
building `ed25519-dalek` via:

`$ cargo build --features="serde"`They can be then serialised into any of the wire formats which serde supports.
For example, using [bincode](https://github.com/TyOverby/bincode):

```
use bincode::serialize;
let encoded_verifying_key: Vec<u8> = serialize(&verifying_key).unwrap();
let encoded_signature: Vec<u8> = serialize(&signature).unwrap();
```
After sending the `encoded_verifying_key` and `encoded_signature`, the
recipient may deserialise them and verify:

```
use bincode::deserialize;
let message: &[u8] = b"This is a test of the tsunami alert system.";
let decoded_verifying_key: VerifyingKey = deserialize(&encoded_verifying_key).unwrap();
let decoded_signature: Signature = deserialize(&encoded_signature).unwrap();
let verified: bool = decoded_verifying_key.verify(&message, &decoded_signature).is_ok();
assert!(verified);
```

# futures - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/futures/^0.3/

## Expand description

Abstractions for asynchronous programming.

This crate provides a number of core abstractions for writing asynchronous code:

- [Futures](https://docs.rs/future/index.html)are single eventual values produced by asynchronous computations. Some programming languages (e.g. JavaScript) call this concept “promise”.
- [Streams](https://docs.rs/stream/index.html)represent a series of values produced asynchronously.
- [Sinks](https://docs.rs/sink/index.html)provide support for asynchronous writing of data.
- [Executors](https://docs.rs/executor/index.html)are responsible for running asynchronous tasks.

The crate also contains abstractions for [asynchronous I/O](https://docs.rs/io/index.html) and
[cross-task communication](https://docs.rs/channel/index.html).

Underlying all of this is the *task system*, which is a form of lightweight
threading. Large asynchronous computations are built up using futures,
streams and sinks, and then spawned as independent tasks that are run to
completion, but *do not block* the thread running them.

The following example describes how the task system context is built and used within macros and keywords such as async and await!.

```
fn main() {
    let pool = ThreadPool::new().expect("Failed to build pool");
    let (tx, rx) = mpsc::unbounded::<i32>();
    // Create a future by an async block, where async is responsible for an
    // implementation of Future. At this point no executor has been provided
    // to this future, so it will not be running.
    let fut_values = async {
        // Create another async block, again where the Future implementation
        // is generated by async. Since this is inside of a parent async block,
        // it will be provided with the executor of the parent block when the parent
        // block is executed.
        //
        // This executor chaining is done by Future::poll whose second argument
        // is a std::task::Context. This represents our executor, and the Future
        // implemented by this async block can be polled using the parent async
        // block's executor.
        let fut_tx_result = async move {
            (0..100).for_each(|v| {
                tx.unbounded_send(v).expect("Failed to send");
            })
        };
        // Use the provided thread pool to spawn the generated future
        // responsible for transmission
        pool.spawn_ok(fut_tx_result);
        let fut_values = rx
            .map(|v| v * 2)
            .collect();
        // Use the executor provided to this async block to wait for the
        // future to complete.
        fut_values.await
    };
    // Actually execute the above future, which will invoke Future::poll and
    // subsequently chain appropriate Future::poll and methods needing executors
    // to drive all futures. Eventually fut_values will be driven to completion.
    let values: Vec<i32> = executor::block_on(fut_values);
    println!("Values={:?}", values);
}
```
The majority of examples and code snippets in this crate assume that they are inside an async block as written above.
